h1: Keeping weevils and moths out of a brewery grain store
title: Keeping Pests Out of the Grain Store | Craft Beer School
desc: How to keep weevils, flour beetles and moths out of a brewery grain store in Indian heat: receiving checks, storage layout, traps and records.
teaser: One infested sack can seed a whole grain store within weeks in Indian heat. Here is how breweries stop it at the door.
standfirst: Stored grain pests thrive in warm, humid conditions, which describes much of India for much of the year. A brewery grain store needs a routine, not a one-off spray. That routine starts before the malt is even unloaded.
sections: The pests you are likely to meet

Most problems in a malt store come from a short list of insects.

  • Rice weevil and granary weevil. Small brown or black beetles with a long snout. The larvae develop inside whole kernels, so infested grain can look normal from the outside.
  • Lesser grain borer. Also bores into whole grain and leaves fine dust behind.
  • Red flour beetle and saw-toothed grain beetle. Feed on broken kernels, flour and mill dust. They love the area around the mill.
  • Indian meal moth. The larvae spin silk webbing across grain surfaces and in sack folds. Adults fly in the evening.

Warmth speeds every life cycle. Many of these insects breed far faster at 30 °C than at 20 °C, which is why a store that was clean in January can be crawling by June.
Stop it at the receiving door

Most infestations arrive with the grain. Inspect every delivery before it goes into the store.

  • Check sacks for holes, webbing, live insects and fine dust in the seams.
  • Open one sack per lot and look at the grain. Sieve a sample through a fine mesh and check what falls through.
  • Smell it. Musty or sour notes suggest damp or insect activity.
  • Record the supplier, lot number and result in a receiving log.

Reject or quarantine anything with live insects. Do not put a suspect sack in the main store and plan to use it first. That is how one lot becomes a store-wide problem.
Store layout that makes pests easy to see

Good storage is mostly about access and visibility.

  • Stack sacks on pallets, never directly on the floor.
  • Leave a gap of around 45 cm between stacks and walls so you can walk round, sweep and inspect. Paint a white line on the floor to mark it.
  • Keep stacks low enough to see the top sacks.
  • Run first in, first out by date, with lot labels facing outward.
  • Keep the store dry and as cool as you can. Shade, ventilation and keeping the grain away from brewhouse steam all help.

Seal gaps around pipes and doors, fit fly screens on windows and keep the door shut. Spent grain, bins and food waste should be kept well away from the grain store.
The mill room is where most trouble starts

Flour beetles feed on fine dust and broken kernels, which a mill produces in quantity. A mill room that is swept once a month is an insect nursery.

Clean the mill and the area around it after every milling session. Vacuum rather than blow with compressed air, which spreads dust into corners. Empty and clean the grist case and any augers or elevators on a fixed schedule, because grain trapped in dead corners is where beetle colonies hide. Mill dust is also a fire and explosion hazard, which is another reason to keep it under control.

Pheromone traps for stored product moths and beetles are inexpensive and give early warning. Place them around the store and mill room at set points, mark each on a site plan and check them weekly.

Log the count for each trap. One moth is information. A count that climbs over three weeks is a signal to search for the source, usually a forgotten sack, a spill under a pallet or a dead corner in the mill. The value is in the trend, not in a single check. This is the same thinking as any part of a quality system for a small brewery.
Bring in a professional and keep records

A licensed pest control contractor should handle rodent control and any chemical treatment. Fumigation of stored grain uses hazardous chemicals and must be done only by trained, licensed operators. Never attempt it yourself.

Ask the contractor for a site plan of bait stations, the products used and a service report after each visit. Keep bait stations outside the production area or in tamper-proof boxes away from open grain. Food safety rules expect pest control to be planned and recorded. An inspector will ask to see the file. Our guide to preparing a brewery for inspection covers what else they look for. Requirements vary by state, so check current rules.

Isolate the affected lot, bag it and remove it from the building. Check neighbouring sacks and the floor beneath. Clean the area thoroughly, then step up trap checks for a few weeks.

Lightly affected grain is sometimes still usable for milling and mashing, because the boil kills insects. But insect fragments and damage bring off flavours and a quality risk. In a commercial brewery the safer rule is simple: if it is crawling, it goes.
faqs: How do weevils get into malt?
Most arrive with the grain from the supplier or warehouse. Inspect every delivery and quarantine any lot with live insects.
Do pheromone traps kill all the insects?
No. They are for monitoring. A rising count tells you where to look for the source, which you then remove and clean.
Can I fumigate my grain store myself?
No. Fumigation chemicals are hazardous and must only be applied by trained, licensed pest control operators.
